mcq.q: Solve: −x + 19 < 7x − 45
mcq.explain: Collect x on the left: (-1 − (7))x < -45 − (19), i.e. -8x < -64. Dividing by -8 (a negative number) reverses the inequality sign: x > 8. Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number is the classic error.
mcq.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
mcq.fast: Test x = 9 (a point on the claimed side) in the original inequality; it must be true.

mcq.q: Solve: −2x − 8 ≤ 6x − 28
mcq.explain: Collect x on the left: (-2 − (6))x ≤ -28 − (-8), i.e. -8x ≤ -20. Dividing by -8 (a negative number) reverses the inequality sign: x ≥ 5/2. Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number is the classic error.
mcq.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
mcq.fast: Test x = 7/2 (a point on the claimed side) in the original inequality; it must be true.

mcq.q: Solve: 5x + 6 < x + 30
mcq.explain: Collect x on the left: (5 − (1))x < 30 − (6), i.e. 4x < 24. Dividing by 4 keeps the sign because it is positive: x < 6. Forgetting to reverse the sign when dividing by a negative number is the classic error.
mcq.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
mcq.fast: Test x = 5 (a point on the claimed side) in the original inequality; it must be true.

mcq.q: How many integers x satisfy -5 < 4x + 6 ≤ 35?
mcq.explain: Subtract 6 and divide every part by 4: -11/4 < x ≤ 29/4. The integers in this range are -2 to 7, which is 10 integers. Check the end points carefully — a strict sign excludes an end point that is itself an integer.
mcq.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
mcq.fast: Integers from -2 to 7: count = 7 − (-2) + 1 = 10.

mcq.q: How many integers x satisfy 6 < 2x < 36?
mcq.explain: Subtract 0 and divide every part by 2: 3 < x < 18. The integers in this range are 4 to 17, which is 14 integers. Check the end points carefully — a strict sign excludes an end point that is itself an integer.
mcq.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
mcq.fast: Integers from 4 to 17: count = 17 − (4) + 1 = 14.

mcq.q: How many integers x satisfy -12 ≤ 2x − 6 ≤ 14?
mcq.explain: Subtract -6 and divide every part by 2: -3 ≤ x ≤ 10. The integers in this range are -3 to 10, which is 14 integers. Check the end points carefully — a strict sign excludes an end point that is itself an integer.
mcq.topic: Inequalities and their rules; one-variable solution space
mcq.fast: Integers from -3 to 10: count = 10 − (-3) + 1 = 14.

mcq.q: Which point lies in the region x + 3y ≤ 31, 3x + 4y ≥ 11, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0?
mcq.explain: A point lies in the common region only if it satisfies every inequality. Substitute each option: (8, 6) gives 26 ≤ 31 and 48 ≥ 11, so it is inside. Each other option breaks at least one of the two conditions, so it lies outside the feasible region.
mcq.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points
mcq.fast: Check the first inequality for all four points, then only the survivors against the second.

mcq.q: The lines x + 2y = 10 and 5x + y = 41 meet at the corner point:
mcq.explain: A corner point of the feasible region where two boundary lines cross is found by solving them as simultaneous equations. Eliminating one variable gives x = 8 and y = 1. Check: 1(8) + 2(1) = 10 and 5(8) + 1(1) = 41. The intercepts on the axes are different corner points.
mcq.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points
mcq.fast: Put each option into both equations; Cramer's rule: x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).

mcq.explain: A corner point of the feasible region where two boundary lines cross is found by solving them as simultaneous equations. Eliminating one variable gives x = 7 and y = 1. Check: 2(7) + 5(1) = 19 and 2(7) + 4(1) = 18. The intercepts on the axes are different corner points.
mcq.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points
mcq.fast: Put each option into both equations; Cramer's rule: x = (c₁b₂ − c₂b₁)/(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁).

mcq.q: Maximise Z = 5x + 4y subject to 5x + 5y ≤ 65, 5x + 3y ≤ 45, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The maximum value of Z is:
mcq.explain: The feasible region has corner points (0, 0), (9, 0), (3, 10) and (0, 13). Evaluate Z at each: 0, 45, 55, 52. The largest is 55 at (3, 10). Using the larger intercept (13, 0) is a trap — that point violates the other constraint.
mcq.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method
mcq.fast: Corner-point method: find the 3 non-zero corners (two intercepts that satisfy both constraints, and the intersection) and compare Z.

mcq.q: Minimise Z = 4x + 3y subject to 5x + y ≥ 80, 5x + 5y ≥ 100, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. The minimum value of Z is:
mcq.explain: With "≥" constraints the feasible region is unbounded, away from the origin. Its corner points are (20, 0), (15, 5) and (0, 80). Z there = 80, 75, 240; the minimum is 75 at (15, 5). Zero is not possible because (0, 0) is outside the region.
mcq.topic: Optimal solution — corner point method and matrix method
mcq.fast: Evaluate Z only at the three corners: the larger x-intercept, the larger y-intercept and the intersection point.

mcq.q: A unit makes x shirts and y pairs of trousers. Each shirt needs 3 hours of labour and each pair of trousers needs 1 hour; only 142 hours of labour are available. The constraint is:
mcq.explain: Total labour used = 3 per unit × x + 1 per unit × y = 3x + y. Usage cannot exceed what is available, so 3x + y ≤ 142. Use "≤" for a limited resource and "≥" for a minimum requirement. Swapping the coefficients attaches each requirement to the wrong product.
mcq.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem
mcq.fast: Coefficient of x goes with the product called x; "only/at most/available" means ≤.

mcq.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem

mcq.q: A firm maximises Z = 3x subject to x + y ≤ 15 (resource P), 2x + 4y ≤ 56 (resource Q), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. At the optimum, how many units of the resource that is not fully used remain unused?
mcq.explain: Z depends only on x, so the optimum is the largest x allowed: x = 15, y = 0 (the binding constraint gives x ≤ 15). The other resource uses 2 × 15 = 30 of its 56 units, so 26 units remain unused (its slack). The binding resource has zero slack.
mcq.topic: Summary of the graphical method and unused resources
mcq.fast: Optimum at the smaller x-intercept (15, 0); unused = capacity − usage = 56 − 30.

mcq.q: A firm maximises Z = 2x subject to 2x + 2y ≤ 44 (resource P), 4x + y ≤ 52 (resource Q), x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0. At the optimum, how many units of the resource that is not fully used remain unused?
mcq.explain: Z depends only on x, so the optimum is the largest x allowed: x = 13, y = 0 (the binding constraint gives x ≤ 13). The other resource uses 2 × 13 = 26 of its 44 units, so 18 units remain unused (its slack). The binding resource has zero slack.
mcq.topic: Summary of the graphical method and unused resources
mcq.fast: Optimum at the smaller x-intercept (13, 0); unused = capacity − usage = 44 − 26.

mcq.q: How many corner points does the feasible region of 2x + y ≤ 28, 5x + 3y ≤ 75, x ≤ 10, x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0 have?
mcq.explain: Draw the two lines using their intercepts, the line x = 10, and keep the side allowed by each sign. The common region is a polygon with corners (0, 0), (0, 25), (9, 10), (10, 0), (10, 8). So it has 5 corner points. Points where lines cross outside the region are not corner points.
mcq.topic: Common region (feasible region) and corner points
mcq.fast: Sketch with intercepts only; test each crossing point in all constraints and count the survivors.

mcq.fast: Sketch with intercepts only; test each crossing point in all constraints and count the survivors.

mcq.q: The solution region of 8x + 7y ≤ 40 is:
options: The half-plane that does not contain the origin
The half-plane that contains the origin
Only the points on the line
mcq.explain: Draw the line 8x + 7y = 40; it divides the plane into two half-planes. Test the origin: 0 ≤ 40 is true, so the solution region is the side containing the origin, together with the line itself (because the sign includes equality).
mcq.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables
mcq.fast: Origin test: put x = 0, y = 0 — true means shade the origin side.

mcq.topic: Graphing a linear inequality in two variables
mcq.fast: Origin test: put x = 0, y = 0 — true means shade the origin side.

mcq.q: A student scored 45, 47, 65 in the first 3 tests. What is the minimum score in test 4 for an average of at least 61?
mcq.explain: Let the score be x. Average ≥ 61 means (45 + 47 + 65 + x)/4 ≥ 61, i.e. 157 + x ≥ 244, so x ≥ 87. The minimum score is 87. Writing x ≥ 61 ignores how the earlier scores pull the average up or down.
mcq.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem
mcq.fast: Total needed = 4 × 61 = 244; subtract the marks already earned (157).

mcq.explain: Let the score be x. Average ≥ 68 means (97 + 43 + 52 + 65 + x)/5 ≥ 68, i.e. 257 + x ≥ 340, so x ≥ 83. The minimum score is 83. Writing x ≥ 68 ignores how the earlier scores pull the average up or down.
mcq.topic: Developing inequalities from a descriptive problem
mcq.fast: Total needed = 5 × 68 = 340; subtract the marks already earned (257).
